pages.why: Relative references must resolve against the final URL after an HTTP redirect.
An empty asynchronously fetched script must not pass a null source pointer to the JavaScript evaluator.
Locks down browser-like request defaults, page-supplied headers, response metadata, cookie persistence, and XHR forwarding against a local server.
A relative specifier must resolve against the importing module's URL, not the page URL, at every hop; and a module-capable client must run the module bundle or the nomodule fallback, never both.
JSON-LD is the page's own record of itself and is present whether or not the application hydrates. A malformed block must be reported rather than dropped, and must not corrupt the extraction output.

pages.why: A recognised bot-challenge shell must be classified before its scripts run. Detecting one is not solving it: the run reports a distinct status instead of spending the settle budget on a page that can never yield content.
Ordinary pages name bot-mitigation vendors without being challenges. Misclassifying one skips the scripts of a working page, so vendor script names must never be treated as evidence of a challenge.

Every other extraction fixture presents one shape cleanly, so nothing asked the classifier what to do when several signals appear at once -- which is what every real page does. An article carrying a site search box, a table, images, and an embed is still an article; deciding on the first matching element classified every encyclopaedia article as its own search form.

The reader renders its own template, so a source document's direction and language must survive extraction or a right-to-left article is laid out flush left. Mixed-direction ordering within the paragraph needs the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm and is recorded rather than asserted.

Japanese and Chinese have no inter-word spaces, so a line may break between almost any two characters subject to kinsoku rules. This is what libunibreak is a dependency for, and no other corpus page exercises it: every other fixture breaks on spaces.

pages.why: Thai has no word delimiter at all and stacks vowels and tone marks on the base consonant; Devanagari reorders within a cluster, so a vowel typed after its consonant is drawn before it. Extraction must preserve both intact; correct shaping is a render-path question recorded rather than asserted.

pages.why: A login is two requests that only validate together: the GET that issues the form cookie and token, then the POST that returns both. Each navigation is a separate engine process, so without a session file the two halves never meet and a signed-in user is signed out by their next click. The steps below run as separate processes sharing only the cookie file; reaching the gated page at all is the assertion.

A front page is headlines that are themselves links, with no article for Readability to find. Without a document title the reader showed 'Untitled page'; without the link on each block it showed headlines nobody could follow; and rendered into a fixed surface the page simply stopped partway down.

A permalink into a stream names one item and ships the whole stream around it, so the item the reader asked for was 2.5% of what the reader rendered. Readability cannot separate them -- it scores the densest container, which is the stream. schema.org hasPart names the region, the item commonly appears twice (pinned and in place), and the page-level block list is grouped by tag, which would split the headline from its paragraphs.

pages.why: A client-side failure must not erase useful server-rendered content from the reader.

pages.why: Known page data can recover ordered content and actions without executing a framework component tree.
Vercel's security checkpoint must be classified as an access challenge instead of being presented as a one-paragraph page.

pages.plan_section: Phase 1 extraction breadth, audio references and direct/embed classification
pages.why: Audio is the one medium the reader plays itself, so it must be extracted from the shapes pages actually use: a <source> child rather than a src attribute, and an enclosure in JSON-LD. The same page pins the direct/embed split that decides whether a video card offers a download or a hand-off, and proves the Audio stub keeps a script-built player from throwing mid-settle.

pages.plan_section: Phase 1 extraction breadth, direct video files and adaptive-stream manifests
pages.why: A <video> carrying only <source> children is the common form, and reading the src attribute alone left the card pointing at nothing. The reader never decodes video, so a direct file must offer a download -- and an HLS manifest must not, because it is a playlist of segments rather than a file.

pages.plan_section: Phase 1 extraction breadth, embedded state survey
pages.why: The survey measures state blobs the reader does not use, which is the evidence a generic embedded-data mapper would be built on. Both shapes here are unmapped on purpose: an assignment-style blob the adapter path never sees, and a JSON-typed one it sees and cannot claim. The gate is that recording them changes nothing about what the reader shows.

pages.plan_section: Phase 1 extraction breadth, audio offered as links
pages.why: A download listing offers audio as links and carries no audio element at all, so a reader that only looks for <audio> can play files it will never show. The same file linked twice must collapse to one reference, a PDF link must not become audio, and a format the core cannot decode must be offered as a download rather than a Play that fails.

pages.plan_section: Phase 1, a resource that is not a document
pages.why: Following a link to a media file handed its bytes to the HTML parser, which produced an empty document and a reader page with no title and nothing on it. The bytes decide what a resource is, as everywhere else here, and what comes back is the same card an embedded reference gets.

pages.plan_section: Minimal computed style, at the size of a real page
pages.why: Extraction asked every element whether the page's stylesheet hid it by copying and re-parsing every <style> element each time, and never returned the copies. The output was right and the cost was the stylesheet's size times the element count: a BBC front page took the engine from 24 to 152 MiB, and this page takes the old engine to 339 MiB against 45 MiB now. Only a budget sees this; every content assertion passes either way.

pages.plan_section: Phase 0 resource limits: a recursion the engine survives
pages.why: The JS stack limit was a flat 8 MiB, the whole of the process's default stack, so QuickJS's stack check never fired first: a page recursing about 4,600 calls deep killed the engine with SIGSEGV. The limit now comes from the real stack less a margin, and the page gets the RangeError a browser would give it.

Blocking scripts are fetched before the settle loop that enforces the cap, and each fetch got the whole cap as its own timeout, even after the cap had passed. Three scripts that never arrive held the engine for three caps; X settled in 13 s against 5. The cap is hard, so the run must end near it however many fetches remain.

pages.plan_section: Network bridge: a limit on transfers at once
pages.why: The engine attached every request as soon as it was made, 46 at once on one live page, and a platform whose network carries a few parallel transfers cannot take that. It now attaches up to --max-fetches (8 by default) and queues the rest, and a blocking script fetched while every slot is taken waits for one instead of opening a ninth (an engine without that measured 9). The page must still get every answer, which the DOM assertions check; the budget checks the limit is real.
A branded title should resolve to the story rather than the news masthead or its discussion.

divergences: Three fixtures require us to behave differently from a conformant browser, each on purpose: 03b (a browser never settles, we cap), 05 (a browser leaves below-fold lazy content unloaded, our fiction loads it), and 08 (a browser falls back to windows-1252 on an undeclared UTF-8 page, we detect). These are the corpus stating the plan's design choices as testable facts.

open_decisions.question: A page explicitly declares us-ascii (-> windows-1252 per the Encoding Standard) but serves UTF-8. Follow the declaration (spec-correct, illegible) or trust the bytes (legible, non-conformant)?
open_decisions.browser_behaviour: mojibake; Chrome is right to do so
